description:
We’re a team of 6 students, who are curious about how the Earth changes and about the data that shows it. For NASA Space Apps we chose Dancing with SARs. Synthetic Aperture Radar sees through clouds, smoke, and darkness, so it can show floods, land movement, deforestation, and crop change that optical satellites miss.

Who we are
We come from [e.g. programming, data science, engineering, design, biology]. We like turning complicated data into tools people can use and understand.
summary:
What we developed: METRIS is a mobile-friendly web app (also packaged as an Android app) that turns satellite radar (SAR) observations into plain-language answers about how a place is changing. For a chosen area, it tracks four factors: surface water, ground movement, vegetation and soil moisture. It shows them on a map and in charts, tests whether a change is larger than measurement noise, projects the trend about three months ahead, and compares areas. A built-in assistant answers questions only from stored data, gives its sources and confidence, and refuses questions the data cannot support.
How it addresses the challenge: SAR data is powerful but hard for non-experts to read. METRIS lets anyone pick a place and dates and see what changed, what may have caused it (each cause labelled supported, not supported or not tested, using real rainfall and temperature records), and what it could mean. It is built for NISAR’s 12-day repeat observations.
Why it matters: farmers, planners and communities need clear information on floods, subsidence and land change, not raw radar files. METRIS keeps the science honest by labelling every dataset as simulated, observed or live.
Transparency: in this version the four radar factors are simulated placeholders. Real NISAR time series can be loaded with the included tool, with no code changes. Live link: https://imkhema6-svg.github.io/metris-app/
details:
METRIS is an interactive map-like app that integrates space observations with AI to deliver insights about what can happen in the future. Its primary goal is to enable users to monitor regions across five essential dimensions: the nature of the environmental change, its spatial scope, its temporal frame, potential natural or anthropogenic causes, and its expected socioeconomic or environmental impacts. It focuses on providing high precision. For the demo, we only used 3 regions to study, which are

1-The Nile Delta

2-The Bengal Delta

3-Rondônia, the Amazon forest

Benefits of the project:-

Multi-domain monitoring: the project measures water, land deformation, and soil tracking on a single platform that is fairly easy to use, eliminating the need for specialized portals.

Predictive capabilities: since the project has data from the past 2 years and from the present, the AI can expect what can happen in the coming years accurately.

Contextual Education: it recommends specific, reviewed NASA data and statistics that correspond to the user’s region, helping him identify phenomena that can occur near him.

Tools, Hardware, and Software used:

HARDWARE

Windows PC (team members’ laptops): used to run Visual Studio Code, the local server, and GitHub.

Android phone: used to open and test the app in Chrome and add it to the home screen.

Cloud computer (Anthropic’s servers, Linux): Helped in building and testing the code.

SOFTWARE

Claude (Anthropic AI assistant): wrote the code, designed the app structure and drafted documentation.

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript: the languages the app is written in. HTML builds the page, CSS styles it for phones, and JavaScript runs the logic, charts, and assistant.

Node.js: runs the local development server and the app’s self-test (about 60 automated checks of the analysis code and assistant).

npm: Node’s package manager, used to run project commands and install Leaflet and Capacitor.

Python 3: runs a helper script that loads real satellite time series from a CSV file.

Leaflet 1.9.4: open-source library that draws the interactive map.

Capacitor: wraps the web app as an Android (or iOS) app.

Android Studio: builds the Android APK file from the Capacitor project.

Playwright (headless Chromium): automated browser testing at phone size, checking every screen for layout problems and errors.

Color validation script: checked the chart colors for color-blind safety and contrast.

Visual Studio Code: the code editor used to run and edit the project.

Git: version control, used to upload the project to GitHub.

GitHub and GitHub Pages: store the code and host the live website, published automatically by a GitHub Actions workflow.

Google Chrome (phone and PC): used to open and test the live app.

ONLINE SERVICES AND DATA

Open-Meteo (ERA5 reanalysis weather data): rainfall, temperature and soil moisture.

NASA GIBS: MODIS satellite imagery on the map.

OpenStreetMap: map tiles.

NOT USED

No paid tools, no database or backend server, and no image-generation or design software. The app icon is our own SVG. Real NISAR data was not processed, and the four radar factors in this version are simulated placeholders.
